claims.text: Increasing phosphorus content by 1–3 at.% relative to a phosphorus-containing alloy baseline will improve glass-forming ability.
Increasing phosphorus content by 1–3 at.% will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
The phosphorus increase should be applied while keeping the other elemental ratios nearly constant.
The beneficial effect is expected only when no competing crystallization-promoting phases are present.
Additional phosphorus will form localized phosphorus-rich clusters.
Phosphorus-rich clusters impede the long-range atomic diffusion required for crystallization.
Increasing phosphorus promotes strong phosphorus-centered bonding environments.
The proposed local phosphorus-centered environments enhance topological frustration and chemical disorder.
Enhanced topological frustration and chemical disorder retard the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
The phosphorus-enriched alloy will have a greater critical casting thickness than the baseline alloy under the same processing conditions.
The phosphorus-enriched alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline alloy.
The benefit should disappear if added phosphorus exceeds its solubility limit or induces undesirable phosphorus-rich crystalline phases.
Phosphorus addition may provide no improvement in systems that segregate upon phosphorus enrichment.
Phosphorus addition may provide no improvement when the baseline amorphous structure is already highly stable.
